THOUGHT: The patient is a 22-year-old male with acute onset of progressive swelling, pain, and functional impairment in the right ring finger after a traumatic “jersey pull” mechanism—classic for a forced hyperextension injury to the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Key clinical findings include: (1) inability to actively flex the DIP joint (i.e., loss of active distal interphalangeal flexion), (2) finger held in extension at rest (suggesting loss of flexor tendon continuity), (3) localized tenderness and swelling at the DIP joint, and (4) absence of fracture or dislocation on X-ray. The mechanism—sudden longitudinal traction on a flexed fingertip (e.g., jersey caught and pulled)—is highly associated with rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at its insertion into the distal phalanx. This is known as a “jersey finger.” The inability to flex the DIP joint against resistance (or even initiate flexion) while proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) motion remain intact strongly localizes the lesion to the FDP tendon. MRI is expected to confirm FDP tendon disruption—typically at the level of the DIP joint or bony avulsion (with or without small bony fragment). Differential diagnoses such as mallet finger (extensor tendon injury) are ruled out because mallet finger presents with *inability to extend* the DIP joint (i.e., DIP flexion deformity), not inability to flex it; here, the finger is extended at rest and cannot flex — the opposite pattern. No neurovascular compromise or systemic signs suggest a non-infectious, purely traumatic etiology.

DIAGNOSIS: Jersey finger (rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon)
ground_truth: Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion
